s://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_time "Civil time") in a particular [time zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_zone "Time zone") can be determined by adding or subtracting the number of hours and minutes specified by the [UTC offset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC_offset "UTC offset"), which ranges from [UTC−12:00](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC−12:00 "UTC−12:00") in the west to [UTC+14:00](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC+14:00 "UTC+14:00") in the east (see [List of UTC offsets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_UTC_offsets "List of UTC offsets")).

The time zone using UTC is sometimes denoted [UTC+00:00](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC+00:00 "UTC+00:00") or by the letter *Z*—a reference to the equivalent [nautical time zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nautical_time "Nautical time") (GMT), which has been denoted by a *Z* since about 1950.[*[by whom?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Words_to_watch#Unsupported_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")*] Time zones were identified by successive letters of the alphabet and the Greenwich time zone was marked by a *Z* as it was the point of origin. The letter also refers to the "zone description" of zero hours, which has been used since 1920 (see [time zone history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_zone#History "Time zone")). Since the [NATO phonetic alphabet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO_phonetic_alphabet "NATO phonetic alphabet") word for *Z* is "Zulu", UTC is sometimes known as "**Zulu time**". This is especially true in aviation, where "Zulu" is the universal standard.[[20]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMilitary_&_Civilian_Time_Designationsn.d.-22) This ensures that all pilots, regardless of location, are using the same [24-hour clock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/24-hour_clock "24-hour clock"), thus avoiding confusion when flying between time zones.[[21]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliams2005-23) See the [list of military time zones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_military_time_zones "List of military time zones") for letters used in addition to *Z* in qualifying time zones other than Greenwich.

On electronic devices which only allow the time zone to be configured using maps or city names, UTC can be selected indirectly by selecting cities such as [Accra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accra "Accra") in [Ghana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana "Ghana") or [Reykjavík](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reykjavík "Reykjavík") in [Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland "Iceland") as they are always on UTC and do not currently use [daylight saving time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daylight_saving_time "Daylight saving time") (which [Greenwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwich "Greenwich") and [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") do, and so could be a source of error).[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEIceland2011-24)

### Daylight saving time

Main article: [Daylight saving time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daylight_saving_time "Daylight saving time")

UTC does not change with a change of seasons, but [local time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_zone "Time zone") or civil time may change if a time zone jurisdiction observes daylight saving time (summer time). For example, local time on the east coast of the United States is five hours behind UTC during winter,[[23]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTE15_U.S._Code_§_2612007-25) but four hours behind while daylight saving is observed there.[[24]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTE15_U.S._Code_§_260a2005-26)

### Timing centers

There are over 70 official UTC timing centers who maintain [atomic clocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_clock "Atomic clock") around the world from which UTC is calculated.[[25]](#cite_note-27) UTC is calculated by the BIPM[[26]](#cite_note-28) using [weighted averages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weighted_arithmetic_mean "Weighted arithmetic mean") of the reports by the timing centers.[[27]](#cite_note-29)[[28]](#cite_note-30) BIPM lists the

## History

Further information: [Universal time § History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_time#History "Universal time")

In 1928, the term *Universal Time* (*UT*) was introduced by the International Astronomical Union to refer to GMT, with the day starting at midnight.[[32]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCarthySeidelmann200910–11-34) Until the 1950s, broadcast [time signals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_signal "Time signal") were based on UT, and hence on the rotation of the Earth.

In 1955, the [caesium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caesium "Caesium") [atomic clock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_clock "Atomic clock") was invented. This provided a form of timekeeping that was both more stable and more convenient than astronomical observations. In 1956, the U.S. [National Bureau of Standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Bureau_of_Standards "National Bureau of Standards") and [U.S. Naval Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Naval_Observatory "U.S. Naval Observatory") started to develop atomic frequency time scales; by 1959, these time scales were used in generating the [WWV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WWV_(radio_station) "WWV (radio station)") time signals, named for the shortwave radio station that broadcasts them. In 1960, the U.S. Naval Observatory, the Royal Greenwich Observatory, and the [UK National Physical Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Physical_Laboratory_(United_Kingdom) "National Physical Laboratory (United Kingdom)") coordinated their radio broadcasts so that time steps and frequency changes were coordinated, and the resulting time scale was informally referred to as "Coordinated Universal Time".[[33]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCarthySeidelmann2009226–227-35)[[34]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCarthy20093-36)

In a controversial decision, the frequency of the signals was initially set to match the rate of UT, but then kept at the same frequency by the use of atomic clocks and deliberately allowed to drift away from UT. When the divergence grew significantly, the signal was phase shifted (stepped) by 20 [ms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millisecond "Millisecond") to bring it back into agreement with UT. Twenty-nine such steps were used before 1960.[[35]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAriasGuinotQuinn2003-37)

In 1958, data was published linking the frequency for the [caesium transition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caesium_standard "Caesium standard"), newly established, with the [ephemeris second](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ephemeris_time "Ephemeris time"). The ephemeris second is a unit in the system of time that, when used as the independent variable in the laws of motion that govern the movement of the planets and moons in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System"), enables the laws of motion to accurately predict the observed positions of Solar System bodies. Within the limits of observable accuracy, ephemeris seconds are of constant length, as are atomic seconds. This publication allowed a value to be chosen for the length of th

evidence.text:
e atomic second that would accord with the celestial laws of motion.[[36]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarkowitzHallEssenParry1958-38)

The coordination of time and frequency transmissions around the world began on 1 January 1960. UTC was first officially adopted in 1963 as [CCIR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITU-R#CCIR "ITU-R") Recommendation 374, *Standard-Frequency and Time-Signal Emissions*, and "UTC" became the official abbreviation of Coordinated Universal Time in 1967.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCarthy20094-4)

In 1961, the [Bureau International de l'Heure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Time_Bureau "International Time Bureau") began coordinating the UTC process internationally (but the name Coordinated Universal Time was not formally adopted by the International Astronomical Union until 1967).[[37]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelsonMcCarthy200515-39)[[38]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelsonMcCarthyMalysLevine2001515-40) From then on, there were time steps every few months, and frequency changes at the end of each year. The jumps increased in size to 0.1 seconds. This UTC was intended to permit a very close approximation to UT2.[[33]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCarthySeidelmann2009226–227-35)

In 1967, the [SI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SI "SI") second was redefined in terms of the frequency supplied by a caesium atomic clock. The length of second so defined was practically equal to the second of ephemeris time.[[39]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarkowitz1988-41) This was the frequency that had been provisionally used in TAI since 1958. It was soon decided that having two types of second with different lengths, namely the UTC second and the SI second used in TAI, was a bad idea. It was thought better for time signals to maintain a consistent frequency, and that this frequency should match the SI second. Thus it would be necessary to rely on time steps alone to maintain the approximation of UT. This was tried experimentally in a service known as "Stepped Atomic Time" (SAT), which ticked at the same rate as TAI and used jumps of 0.2 seconds to stay synchronised with UT2.[[40]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCarthySeidelmann2009227-42)

There was also dissatisfaction with the frequent jumps in UTC (and SAT). In 1968, [Louis Essen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Essen "Louis Essen"), the inventor of the caesium atomic clock, and G. M. R. Winkler both independently proposed that steps should be of 1 second only.[[41]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEssen1968161–165-43) to simplify future adjustments. This system was eventually approved as [leap seconds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leap_second "Leap second") in a new UTC in 1970 and implemented in 1972, along with the idea of maintaining the UTC second equal to the TAI second. This CCIR Recommendation 460 "stated that (a) carrier frequencies and time intervals should be maintained constant and should correspond to the definition of the [SI second](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SI_second "SI second"); (b) step adjustments, when necessary, should be exactly 1 s to maintain approximate agreement with Universal Time (UT); and (c) standard signals should contain information on the difference between UTC and UT."[[42]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCarthy20095-44)

As an intermediate step at the end of 1971, there was a final irregular jump of exactly 0.107758 TAI seconds, making the total of all the small time steps and frequency shifts in UTC or TAI during 1958–1971 exactly ten seconds, so that 1 January 1972 00:00:00 UTC was 1 January 1972 00:00:10 TAI exactly,[[43]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair197432-45) and a whole number of seconds thereafter. At the same time, the tick rate of UTC was changed to exactly match TAI. UTC also started to track UT1 rather than UT2. Some time signals started to broadcast the DUT1 correction (UT1 − UTC) for applications requiring a closer approximation of UT1 than UTC provided.[[44]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESeidelmann199285–87-46)[[45]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelsonLombardiOkayama200546-47)

The current vers

ion of UTC is defined by [International Telecommunication Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Telecommunication_Union "International Telecommunication Union") Recommendation (ITU-R TF.460-6), *Standard-frequency and time-signal emissions*,[[46]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEITU_Radiocommunication_Assembly2002-48) and is based on [International Atomic Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Atomic_Time "International Atomic Time") (TAI) with leap seconds added at irregular intervals to compensate for the accumulated difference between TAI and time measured by [Earth's rotation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_rotation "Earth's rotation").[[47]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChester2015-49) Leap seconds are inserted as necessary to keep UTC within 0.9 seconds of the [UT1 variant of universal time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_time#Versions "Universal time").[[48]](#cite_note-50) See [§ Current number of leap seconds](#Current_number_of_leap_seconds) for the number of leap seconds inserted to date.

### Current number of leap seconds

The first leap second occurred on 30 June 1972. Since then, leap seconds have occurred on average about once every 19 months, always on 30 June or 31 December. As of July 2022[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Coordinated_Universal_Time&action=edit), there have been 27 leap seconds in total, all positive, putting UTC 37 seconds behind TAI.[[49]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBulletin_C2022-51)

A study published in March 2024 in *[Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature_(journal) "Nature (journal)")* found that accelerated melting of ice in Greenland and Antarctica due to climate change has slowed Earth's rotation enough to delay the next negative leap-second adjustment to UTC, postponing problems for computer systems.[[50]](#cite_note-Nature_20240327-52)

## Rationale

Earth's [rotational speed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotational_speed "Rotational speed") is very slowly decreasing because of [tidal deceleration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tidal_acceleration "Tidal acceleration"); this increases the length of the [mean solar day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_time "Solar time"). The length of the SI second was calibrated on the basis of the second of [ephemeris time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ephemeris_time "Ephemeris time")[[36]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarkowitzHallEssenParry1958-38)[[39]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarkowitz1988-41) and can now be seen to have a relationship with the mean solar day observed between 1750 and 1892, analysed by [Simon Newcomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Newcomb "Simon Newcomb"). As a result, the SI second is close to ⁠1/86400⁠ of a mean solar day in the mid‑19th century.[[51]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCarthySeidelmann200987-53) In earlier centuries, the mean solar day was shorter than 86,400 SI seconds, and in more recent centuries it is longer than 86,400 seconds. Near the end of the 20th century, the length of the mean solar day (also known simply as "length of day" or "LOD") was approximately 86,400.0013 s.[[52]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCarthySeidelmann200954-54) For this reason, UT is now "slower" than TAI by the difference (or "excess" LOD) of 1.3 ms/day.

The excess of the LOD over the nominal 86,400 s accumulates over time, causing the UTC day, initially synchronised with the mean sun, to become desynchronised and run ahead of it. Near the end of the 20th century, with the LOD at 1.3 ms above the nominal value, UTC ran faster than UT by 1.3 ms per day, getting a second ahead roughly every 800 days. Thus, leap seconds were inserted at approximately this interval, retarding UTC to keep it synchronised in the long term.[[53]](#cite_note-55) The actual [rotational period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotation_period "Rotation period") varies on unpredictable factors such as [tectonic motion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plate_tectonics "Plate tectonics") and has to be observed, rather than computed.

Just as adding a le
evidence.title: Coordinated Universal Time - Wikipedia

evidence.text:
ap day every four years does not mean the year is getting longer by one day every four years, the insertion of a leap second every 800 days does not indicate that the mean solar day is getting longer by a second every 800 days. It will take about 50,000 years for a mean solar day to lengthen by one second (at a rate of 2 ms per century). This rate fluctuates within the range of 1.7–2.3 ms/cy. While the rate due to [tidal friction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tidal_friction "Tidal friction") alone is about 2.3 ms/cy, the [uplift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-glacial_rebound "Post-glacial rebound") of [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada") and [Scandinavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scandinavia "Scandinavia") by several metres since the [last ice age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Glacial_Period "Last Glacial Period") has temporarily reduced this to 1.7 ms/cy over the last 2,700 years.[[54]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStephensonMorrison1995-56) The correct reason for leap seconds, then, is not the current difference between actual and nominal LOD, but rather the *accumulation* of this difference over a period of time: Near the end of the 20th century, this difference was about ⁠1/800⁠ of a second per day; therefore, after about 800 days, it accumulated to 1 second (and a leap second was then added).

In the graph of [DUT1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DUT1 "DUT1") above, the excess of LOD above the nominal 86,400 s corresponds to the downward slope of the graph between vertical segments. (The slope became shallower in the 1980s, 2000s and late 2010s to 2020s because of slight accelerations of Earth's rotation temporarily shortening the day.) Vertical position on the graph corresponds to the accumulation of this difference over time, and the vertical segments correspond to leap seconds introduced to match this accumulated difference. Leap seconds are timed to keep DUT1 within the vertical range depicted by the adjacent graph. The frequency of leap seconds therefore corresponds to the slope of the diagonal graph segments, and thus to the excess LOD. Time periods when the slope reverses direction (slopes upwards, not the vertical segments) are times when the excess LOD is negative, that is, when the LOD is below 86,400 s.

## Future

See also: [Leap second](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leap_second "Leap second")

As the Earth's rotation continues to slow, positive leap seconds will be required more frequently. The long-term [rate of change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derivative "Derivative") of LOD is approximately +1.7 ms per century. At the end of the 21st century, LOD will be roughly 86,400.004 s, requiring a leap second about every 250 days. Over several centuries, the frequency of leap seconds will become problematic.[[55]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCarthySeidelmann2009232-57) A change in the trend of the UT1 − UTC values was seen beginning around June 2019 in which instead of slowing down (with leap seconds to keep the difference between UT1 and UTC less than 0.9 seconds) the Earth's rotation has sped up, causing this difference to increase. If the trend continues, a negative leap second may be required, which has not been used before.[[56]](#cite_note-58)[[57]](#cite_note-59)

Some time in the 22nd century, two leap seconds will be required every year. The current practice of only allowing leap seconds in June and December will be insufficient to maintain a difference of less than 1 second, and it might be decided to introduce leap seconds in March and September. In the 25th century, four leap seconds are projected to be required every year, so the current quarterly options would be insufficient.

In April 2001, Rob Seaman of the [National Optical Astronomy Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Optical_Astronomy_Observatory "National Optical Astronomy Observatory") proposed that leap seconds be allowed to be added monthly rather than twice yearly.[[58]](#cite_note-60)

In 2022 a resolu
evidence.title: Coordinated Universal Time - Wikipedia

evidence.text:
tion was adopted by the General Conference on Weights and Measures to redefine UTC and abolish leap seconds, but keep the civil second constant and equal to the SI second, so that [sundials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sundial "Sundial") would slowly get further and further out of sync with civil time. The leap seconds will be eliminated by 2035. The resolution does not break the connection between UTC and UT1, but increases the maximum allowable difference. The details of what the maximum difference will be and how corrections will be implemented is left for future discussions.[[3]](#cite_note-CGPM2022-5) This will result in a shift of the sun's movements relative to civil time, with the difference increasing quadratically with time (i.e., proportional to elapsed centuries squared). This is analogous to the shift of [seasons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Season "Season") relative to the yearly calendar that results from the calendar year not precisely matching the [tropical year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_year "Tropical year") length. This would be a change in civil timekeeping, and would have a slow effect at first but become drastic over several centuries. UTC (and TAI) would be more and more ahead of UT; it would coincide with local mean time along a meridian drifting eastward faster and faster.[[59]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEIrvine2008-61) Thus, the time system will lose its fixed connection to the geographic coordinates based on the [IERS meridian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IERS_Reference_Meridian "IERS Reference Meridian"). The difference between UTC and UT would reach 0.5 hours after the year 2600 and 6.5 hours around 4600.[[60]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllen2011a-62)

[ITU-R](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITU-R "ITU-R") Study Group 7 and Working Party 7A were unable to reach consensus on whether to advance the proposal to the 2012 Radiocommunications Assembly; the chairman of Study Group 7 elected to advance the question to the 2012 Radiocommunications Assembly (20 January 2012),[[61]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESeidelmannSeago2011S190-63) but consideration of the proposal was postponed by the ITU until the World Radio Conference in 2015.[[62]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeap_decision_postponed2012-64) This conference, in turn, considered the question,[[63]](#cite_note-65) but no permanent decision was reached; it only chose to engage in further study with the goal of reconsideration in 2023.[[64]](#cite_note-itu.int-66)[*[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")*]

A proposed alternative to the leap second is the leap hour or leap minute, which requires changes only once every few centuries.[[65]](#cite_note-67)

The ITU World Radiocommunication Conference 2023 (WRC-23), which was held in Dubai (United Arab Emirates) from 20 November to 15 December 2023, formally recognised Resolution 4[[66]](#cite_note-68) of the 27th CGPM (2022), which decides that the maximum value for the difference (UT1 − UTC) will be increased in or before 2035.[[67]](#cite_note-69)

# UTC: The World’s Time Standard

Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) is the basis for civil time in all time zones worldwide.

![Image 2: Portrait of Anne](https://c.tadst.com/gfx/64x64/staff-anne-no-bg.png?1)![Image 3: Portrait of Konstantin](https://c.tadst.com/gfx/64x64/staff-konst-no-bg.png?1)

By [Anne Buckle](https://www.timeanddate.com/company/by/anne-buckle) and [Konstantin Bikos](https://www.timeanddate.com/company/by/konstantin-bikos)

Share this article

![Image 4: Time zone map illustration showing time zones for the whole world.](https://c.tadst.com/gfx/900x506/time-zones-world-map--no-country-abbrev.png?1)

The time in every time zone worldwide is defined by its difference, or offset, from UTC. 

©timeanddate.com

## Point of Reference for Local Times Everywhere

UTC is the time standard commonly used to **determine local times** around the world. Every [time zone](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/time-zones.html) is defined by its difference from UTC, known as its **UTC offset**.

For example, the local time in China is [eight hours ahead of UTC](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/china/one-time-zone.html), so [China Standard Time](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/zones/cst-china) has a UTC offset of UTC+8. When it’s 09

[Our complete guide to UTC offsets](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/utc-offsets.html)[UTC offsets of all time zones](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/zones/)

[![Image 5: Illustrated map of the world's time zones.](https://c.tadst.com/gfx/300x168/tz-map-1518922800.png?1) Time Zone Map Current local times around the world, including (DST) changes.](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/map/)

## UTC Offset Can Shift

While every time zone has a fixed UTC offset, some countries **jump back and forth** from one time zone to another every year, so the local UTC offset shifts accordingly.

This may sound strange, but if you live in a country that observes [Daylight Saving Time](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/dst/about.html) (DST), shifting your UTC offset is precisely what you do every time you [spring ahead or fall back](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/dst/spring-forward-fall-back.html).

People in New York, for example, follow [Eastern Standard Time](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/zones/est) (EST) during part of the year. It’s five hours behind UTC, so the offset is UTC-5. In early March, clocks go ahead by one hour to [Eastern Daylight Time](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/zones/edt) (EDT), reducing the offset to UTC-4.

If you’re the visual type, check out our [Time Zone Map](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/map/)—it reflects all DST changes worldwide in real time.

## 24-Hour Notation

While you’re free to state any time around the world using the [12-hour time format](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/am-and-pm.html) with “am” and “pm” labels, **UTC always uses the 24-hour clock**, also known as [military time](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/military-time.html).

For example, 7 o’clock in the evening must be written as 19:00 UTC. It is incorrect to write 7:00 pm UTC.

[12-hour to 24-hour conversion chart](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/military-time.html#chart)[ISO 8601 is the global standard for time and date formats](https://www.timeanddate.com/calendar/what-is-iso-8601.html)

### GMT: Same, but Different

You may have seen [Greenwich Mean Time](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/zones/gmt) (GMT) being used as a reference point **instead of UTC**. In practice, it doesn’t make any difference: GMT and UTC share the same current time, so both offsets are the same. Technically, however, it’s wrong: [GMT is a time zone, not a time standard](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/gmt-utc-time.html).

More importantly, it can **lead to confusion**. You see, GMT is generally associated with the [local time in the UK](https://www.timeanddate.com/worldclock/uk)—as the name suggests, it reflects the time in Greenwich, London. What some people don’t realize is that the **UK doesn’t observe GMT** during the Daylight Saving Time period, when Brits turn their clocks to [British Summer Time](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/zones/bst) (BST).

BST is one hour ahead of GMT (UTC+1). If you fail to account for that, your [time zone conversion](https://www.timeanddate.com/worldclock/converter.html) will be **one hour off**.

Advertising  

## How UTC Is Measured

Given that so much depends on UTC, it’s no surprise that significant effort goes into ensuring its precision.

**Two components** are used to keep it ticking at exactly the right pace:

*   [International Atomic Time](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/international-atomic-time.html) (TAI): A time scale that combines the output of some 450 [highly precise atomic clocks](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/how-do-atomic-clocks-work.html) worldwide.  
*   [Universal Time](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/universal-time.html) (UT1): Also known as astronomical time or solar time, it refers to the Earth’s rotation. It is used to compare the pace provided by TAI with the actual [length of a day on Earth](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/earth-rotation.html).  

To reconcile the ultra-precise spe

ed of atomic clocks with the fluctuations of Earth’s rotation, a [leap second](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/leapseconds.html) is added to [or removed from](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/negative-leap-second.html) UTC when the **difference between the two components** is predicted to reach 0.9 seconds within 12 months.

[Leap seconds may soon be a thing of the past](https://www.timeanddate.com/news/astronomy/end-of-leap-seconds-2022)

![Image 6: Illustration image](https://c.tadst.com/gfx/600x337/bein-nullmeridian-greenwich.jpg?1)

The Prime Meridian in Greenwich, England. The slip-ons are in the Western Hemisphere, and the sneakers are in the Eastern Hemisphere.

©iStockphoto.com/Kateryna Syta

## UTC Started in the Seventies

Coordinated Universal Time in its present form was **officially adopted on January 1, 1972**.

The concept was developed by the International Radio Consultative Committee (CCIR) in the early sixties. In 1967, the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) officially adopted the name UTC, and in 1970, international agreements were reached to set the legal framework for its worldwide implementation.

[Why it’s so hard to convert time zones in your head](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/convert-time-zones-in-your-head.html)
## GMT Used to Be the Global Standard

Although UTC in its present form has only been around for a few decades, the general idea of using a universal time standard to anchor local times worldwide was first put into practice **as early as 1884**: At the International Meridian Conference, delegates from 25 countries designated **Greenwich Mean Time (GMT) as the reference point**.

## An Unusual Abbreviation

You may have noticed that the letters UTC don’t reflect the order of the words **C**oordinated **U**niversal **T**ime.

[Find out why](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/utc-abbreviation.html)

This historical decision is why GMT is still occasionally used as a substitute for UTC today.

At the time, GMT was **based on Earth’s rotation**—specifically, on the mean solar time at the [prime meridian](https://www.timeanddate.com/geography/prime-meridian-wrong.html), which runs through the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, [London](https://www.timeanddate.com/worldclock/uk/london).

With [advances in timekeeping technology](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/history-of-timekeeping.html) and the need for a more precise and stable global time standard, **UTC eventually replaced GMT**. Today, GMT is just another time zone derived from UTC and is no longer based on solar time in Greenwich.

[What is lunar time?](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/what-is-lunar-time.html)

Difference between UTC and local standard time

|  |
| --- |
| This article **needs [more citations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")**. Please help [improve this article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:EditPage/UTC_offset "Special:EditPage/UTC offset") by [adding citations to reliable sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Referencing_for_beginners "Help:Referencing for beginners"). Unsourced material may be challenged and [removed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Burden_of_evidence "Wikipedia:Verifiability"). *Find sources:* ["UTC offset"](https://www.google.com/search?as_eq=wikipedia&q=%22UTC+offset%22) – [news](https://www.google.com/search?tbm=nws&q=%22UTC+offset%22+-wikipedia&tbs=ar:1) **·** [newspapers](https://www.google.com/search?&q=%22UTC+offset%22&tbs=bkt:s&tbm=bks) **·** [books](https://www.google.com/search?tbs=bks:1&q=%22UTC+offset%22+-wikipedia) **·** [scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=%22UTC+offset%22) **·** [JSTOR](https://www.jstor.org/action/doBasicSearch?Query=%22UTC+offset%22&acc=on&wc=on) *(December 2024)* *([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance_template_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))* |

The **UTC offset** is the difference in hours and minutes between [Coordinated Universal Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time "Coordinated Universal Time") (UTC) and the [standard time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_time "Standard time") at a particular place.[[1]](#cite_note-1) This difference is expressed with respect to UTC and is generall
evidence.title: UTC offset - Wikipedia

evidence.text:
y shown in the format ±[hh]:[mm], ±[hh][mm], or ±[hh]. So if the time being described is two hours ahead of UTC (such as in [Kigali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kigali "Kigali"), [Rwanda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwanda "Rwanda") [approximately 30° E]), the UTC offset would be "+02:00", "+0200", or simply "+02".

By convention, every inhabited place in the world has a UTC offset that is a multiple of 15 minutes but the majority of offsets are stated in whole hours. There are many cases where the national [standard time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_time "Standard time") uses a UTC offset that is not defined solely by longitude.[[a]](#cite_note-2)

## Time zones and time offsets

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=UTC_offset&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Time zones and time offsets")]

Main article: [Time zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_zone "Time zone")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/88/World_Time_Zones_Map.png/500px-World_Time_Zones_Map.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:World_Time_Zones_Map.png)

World map of current time zones

A *[time zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_zone "Time zone")* is a geographical [region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Region "Region") in which residents observe the same [standard time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_time "Standard time"). Although nominally a new time zone is established every 15 degrees east or west of the [prime meridian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_meridian "Prime meridian") (meaning a one-hour change in the time), in practice local geographical or political considerations may vary its application. The most extreme example of this is [time in China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_in_China "Time in China"), which applies a single standard time offset of [UTC+08:00](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC+08:00 "UTC+08:00") (eight hours ahead of [Coordinated Universal Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time "Coordinated Universal Time")), even though China spans five geographical [time zones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_zones "Time zones").

The UTC offset (or **time offset**) is an amount of time added to [Coordinated Universal Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time "Coordinated Universal Time") (UTC) time to specify the time at a given location.

### Daylight saving time

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=UTC_offset&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Daylight saving time")]

Main articles: [Daylight saving time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daylight_saving_time "Daylight saving time"), [Standard time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_time "Standard time"), and [Civil time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_time "Civil time")

Several regions of the world use [daylight saving time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daylight_saving_time "Daylight saving time") (DST) and the UTC offset during this season is typically obtained by adding one hour to local standard time. [Central European Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_European_Time "Central European Time") [UTC+01:00](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC+01:00 "UTC+01:00") is replaced by [Central European Summer Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_European_Summer_Time "Central European Summer Time") [UTC+02:00](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC+02:00 "UTC+02:00"), and Pacific Standard Time [UTC−08:00](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC−08:00 "UTC−08:00") is replaced by Pacific Daylight Time [UTC−07:00](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC−07:00 "UTC−07:00").

This set of cities has been chosen to illustrate the difference between local time and UTC, because they are as close as practicable

**UTC+08:00** is an identifier for a [time offset from UTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC_offset "UTC offset") of +08:00. In [ISO 8601](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_8601 "ISO 8601"), the associated time would be written as 2026-10-02T23:00:36[+08:00](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC+08:00). It is eight hours ahead of [UTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC "UTC"), meaning that when the time in UTC is midnight (00:00), the time in areas using the time zone would be 08:00.

It is the most populous [time zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_zone "Time zone") in the world, as well as a possible candidate for [ASEAN Common Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ASEAN_Common_Time "ASEAN Common Time"), mainly due to China's large population, with an estimated population of 1.4 billion people.

This time zone is used in all predominantly [Chinese-speaking regions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese-speaking_world "Chinese-speaking world"), giving international Chinese websites and TV channels the same time.

The time zone is known as **Central Indonesian Time** ([Indonesian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesian_language "Indonesian language"): *Waktu Indonesia Tengah/WITA*) in Indonesia, **Australian Western Standard Time** in Australia, and **Irkutsk Time** ([Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_language "Russian language"): Иркутское время) or **MSK+5** ([Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_language "Russian language"): МСК+5) in [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia").

## Discrepancies between official UTC+08:00 and geographical UTC+08:00

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=UTC%2B08:00&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Discrepancies between official UTC+08:00 and geographical UTC+08:00")]

This section is only partly updated for longitudes using other time zones. This concerns areas within 112°30′ E to 127°30′ E longitude.

* Parts of Russia, including very easternmost parts of [Krasnoyarsk Krai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krasnoyarsk_Krai "Krasnoyarsk Krai"), where UTC+07:00 is used, and [Zabaykalsky Krai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zabaykalsky_Krai "Zabaykalsky Krai") and most of western [Sakha Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sakha_Republic "Sakha Republic") where UTC+09:00 is used.
* Parts of Indonesia, including eastern [East Java](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Java "East Java") with its capital city [Surabaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surabaya "Surabaya"), most of [Central Kalimantan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Kalimantan "Central Kalimantan") with its capital city [Palangka Raya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palangka_Raya "Palangka Raya"), and eastern part of [West Kalimantan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Kalimantan "West Kalimantan"), where UTC+07:00 is used, and some of the western islands in the province of [Maluku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maluku_(province) "Maluku (province)") and [North Maluku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Maluku "North Maluku") where UTC+09:00 is used.
* East Timor, where UTC+09:00 is used.
* Parts of [Okinawa Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okinawa_Prefecture "Okinawa Prefecture"), Japan, including [Sakishima Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sakishima_Islands "Sakishima Islands") with its westernmost point [Yonaguni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yonaguni "Yonaguni"), western parts of [Kerama Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerama_Islands "Kerama Islands"), and some islands of the western [Okinawa Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okinawa_Islands "Okinawa Islands"), where UTC+09:00 is used.
* The western parts of [Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korea "Korea"), including the North Korean capital city, [Pyongyang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyongyang "Pyongyang") and South Korean capital city, [Seoul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seoul "Seoul"), where UTC+09:00 is used.

## Historical time offsets

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=UTC%2B08:00&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Historical time offsets")]

The southern half of Vietnam ([Republic of Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Vietnam "Republic of Vietnam")) was formerly part of this time zone prior to the national reunification on 30 April 1975, making it one hour ahead of [North Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Vietnam "North Vietnam"). After 1975, the whole country came under the North Vietnamese time zone, UTC+07:00.

According to Presidential Decree 41/1987, Indonesia's ex-province of Timor Timur used this time zone with neighboring East Nusa Tenggara and other provinces in Lesser Sunda Islands, parts of Kalimantan and Sulawesi[[9]](#cite_note-9) until independence as [East Timor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Timor "East Timor"), which the country changed to UTC+09:00 as the official time zone. In addition, [West Kalimantan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Kalimantan "West Kalimantan") and [Central Kalimantan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Kalimantan "Central Kalimantan"), which previously used this time zone, switched to UTC+07:00 ([Western Indonesian Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_in_Indonesia "Time in Indonesia")), following Java and Sumatra.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

It is observed in the **CIST**, **PST** during standard time, and in the **AKDT** during the other months (Daylight saving time).

HomeTime Zones UTC - Time Standard

# UTC: The World’s Time Standard

Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) is the basis for civil time in all time zones worldwide.

Image 2: Portrait of AnneImage 3: Portrait of Konstantin

By Anne Buckle and Konstantin Bikos

Share this article

Image 4: Time zone map illustration showing time zones for the whole world.

The time in every time zone worldwide is defined by its difference, or offset, from UTC. 

©timeanddate.com

## Point of Reference for Local Times Everywhere

UTC is the time standard commonly used to determine local times around the world. Every time zone is defined by its difference from UTC, known as its UTC offset. [...] For example, the local time in China is eight hours ahead of UTC, so China Standard Time has a UTC offset of UTC+8. When it’s 09:00 UTC, clocks in Beijing show 17:00 (5:00 pm).

Our complete guide to UTC offsetsUTC offsets of all time zones

Image 5: Illustrated map of the world's time zones. Time Zone Map Current local times around the world, including (DST) changes.

## UTC Offset Can Shift

While every time zone has a fixed UTC offset, some countries jump back and forth from one time zone to another every year, so the local UTC offset shifts accordingly.

This may sound strange, but if you live in a country that observes Daylight Saving Time (DST), shifting your UTC offset is precisely what you do every time you spring ahead or fall back. [...] People in New York, for example, follow Eastern Standard Time (EST) during part of the year. It’s five hours behind UTC, so the offset is UTC-5. In early March, clocks go ahead by one hour to Eastern Daylight Time (EDT), reducing the offset to UTC-4.

If you’re the visual type, check out our Time Zone Map—it reflects all DST changes worldwide in real time.

## 24-Hour Notation

While you’re free to state any time around the world using the 12-hour time format with “am” and “pm” labels, UTC always uses the 24-hour clock, also known as military time.

For example, 7 o’clock in the evening must be written as 19:00 UTC. It is incorrect to write 7:00 pm UTC.

12-hour to 24-hour conversion chartISO 8601 is the global standard for time and date formats

### GMT: Same, but Different [...] ### GMT: Same, but Different

You may have seen Greenwich Mean Time (GMT) being used as a reference point instead of UTC. In practice, it doesn’t make any difference: GMT and UTC share the same current time, so both offsets are the same. Technically, however, it’s wrong: GMT is a time zone, not a time standard.

More importantly, it can lead to confusion. You see, GMT is generally associated with the local time in the UK—as the name suggests, it reflects the time in Greenwich, London. What some people don’t realize is that the UK doesn’t observe GMT during the Daylight Saving Time period, when Brits turn their clocks to British Summer Time (BST).

BST is one hour ahead of GMT (UTC+1). If you fail to account for that, your time zone conversion will be one hour off.

Advertising [...] Advertising  

## How UTC Is Measured

Given that so much depends on UTC, it’s no surprise that significant effort goes into ensuring its precision.

Two components are used to keep it ticking at exactly the right pace:

   International Atomic Time (TAI): A time scale that combines the output of some 450 highly precise atomic clocks worldwide.  
   Universal Time (UT1): Also known as astronomical time or solar time, it refers to the Earth’s rotation. It is used to compare the pace provided by TAI with the actual length of a day on Earth.  

To reconcile the ultra-precise speed of atomic clocks with the fluctuations of Earth’s rotation, a leap second is added to or removed from UTC when the difference between the two components is predicted to reach 0.9 seconds within 12 months.

evidence.text:
The UTC offset is the difference in hours and minutes between Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) and the standard time at a particular place. This difference is expressed with respect to UTC and is generally shown in the format ±[hh]:[mm], ±[hh][mm], or ±[hh]. So if the time being described is two hours ahead of UTC (such as in Kigali, Rwanda [approximately 30° E]), the UTC offset would be "+02:00", "+0200", or simply "+02".

By convention, every inhabited place in the world has a UTC offset that is a multiple of 15 minutes but the majority of offsets are stated in whole hours. There are many cases where the national standard time uses a UTC offset that is not defined solely by longitude.

## Time zones and time offsets

[edit]

Main article: Time zone [...] [edit]

Main article: Time zone

, in practice local geographical or political considerations may vary its application. The most extreme example of this is time in China, which applies a single standard time offset of UTC+08:00 (eight hours ahead of Coordinated Universal Time), even though China spans five geographical time zones.

The UTC offset (or time offset) is an amount of time added to Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) time to specify the time at a given location.

### Daylight saving time

[edit]

Main articles: Daylight saving time, Standard time, and Civil time [...] Several regions of the world use daylight saving time (DST) and the UTC offset during this season is typically obtained by adding one hour to local standard time. Central European Time UTC+01:00 is replaced by Central European Summer Time UTC+02:00, and Pacific Standard Time UTC−08:00 is replaced by Pacific Daylight Time UTC−07:00.

![Image 6: Illustration image](https://c.tadst.com/gfx/600x337/bein-nullmeridian-greenwich.jpg?1)

The Prime Meridian in Greenwich, England. The slip-ons are in the Western Hemisphere, and the sneakers are in the Eastern Hemisphere.

©iStockphoto.com/Kateryna Syta

## UTC Started in the Seventies

Coordinated Universal Time in its present form was **officially adopted on January 1, 1972**.

The concept was developed by the International Radio Consultative Committee (CCIR) in the early sixties. In 1967, the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) officially adopted the name UTC, and in 1970, international agreements were reached to set the legal framework for its worldwide implementation.

[Why it’s so hard to convert time zones in your head](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/convert-time-zones-in-your-head.html)
## GMT Used to Be the Global Standard

Although UTC in its present form has only been around for a few decades, the general idea of using a universal time standard to anchor local times worldwide was first put into practice **as early as 1884**: At the International Meridian Conference, delegates from 25 countries designated **Greenwich Mean Time (GMT) as the reference point**.

## An Unusual Abbreviation

You may have noticed that the letters UTC don’t reflect the order of the words **C**oordinated **U**niversal **T**ime.

[Find out why](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/utc-abbreviation.html)

This historical decision is why GMT is still occasionally used as a substitute for UTC today.

At the time, GMT was **based on Earth’s rotation**—specifically, on the mean solar time at the [prime meridian](https://www.timeanddate.com/geography/prime-meridian-wrong.html), which runs through the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, [London](https://www.timeanddate.com/worldclock/uk/london).

With [advances in timekeeping technology](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/history-of-timekeeping.html) and the need for a more precise and stable global time standard, **UTC eventually replaced GMT**. Today, GMT is just another time zone derived from UTC and is no longer based on solar time in Greenwich.

[What is lunar time?](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/what-is-lunar-time.html)

segments.text:
HomeTime Zones UTC - Time Standard

# UTC: The World’s Time Standard

Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) is the basis for civil time in all time zones worldwide.

Image 2: Portrait of AnneImage 3: Portrait of Konstantin

By Anne Buckle and Konstantin Bikos

Share this article

Image 4: Time zone map illustration showing time zones for the whole world.

The time in every time zone worldwide is defined by its difference, or offset, from UTC. 

©timeanddate.com

## Point of Reference for Local Times Everywhere

UTC is the time standard commonly used to determine local times around the world. Every time zone is defined by its difference from UTC, known as its UTC offset. [...] For example, the local time in China is eight hours ahead of UTC, so China Standard Time has a UTC offset of UTC+8. When it’s 09:00 UTC, clocks in Beijing show 17:00 (5:00 pm).

Our complete guide to UTC offsetsUTC offsets of all time zones

Image 5: Illustrated map of the world's time zones. Time Zone Map Current local times around the world, including (DST) changes.

## UTC Offset Can Shift

While every time zone has a fixed UTC offset, some countries jump back and forth from one time zone to another every year, so the local UTC offset shifts accordingly.

This may sound strange, but if you live in a country that observes Daylight Saving Time (DST), shifting your UTC offset is precisely what you do every time you spring ahead or fall back. [...] People in New York, for example, follow Eastern Standard Time (EST) during part of the year. It’s five hours behind UTC, so the offset is UTC-5. In early March, clocks go ahead by one hour to Eastern Daylight Time (EDT), reducing the offset to UTC-4.

If you’re the visual type, check out our Time Zone Map—it reflects all DST changes worldwide in real time.

## 24-Hour Notation

While you’re free to state any time around the world using the 12-hour time format with “am” and “pm” labels, UTC always uses the 24-hour clock, also known as military time.

For example, 7 o’clock in the evening must be written as 19:00 UTC. It is incorrect to write 7:00 pm UTC.

12-hour to 24-hour conversion chartISO 8601 is the global standard for time and date formats

### GMT: Same, but Different [...] ### GMT: Same, but Different

You may have seen Greenwich Mean Time (GMT) being used as a reference point instead of UTC. In practice, it doesn’t make any difference: GMT and UTC share the same current time, so both offsets are the same. Technically, however, it’s wrong: GMT is a time zone, not a time standard.

More importantly, it can lead to confusion. You see, GMT is generally associated with the local time in the UK—as the name suggests, it reflects the time in Greenwich, London. What some people don’t realize is that the UK doesn’t observe GMT during the Daylight Saving Time period, when Brits turn their clocks to British Summer Time (BST).

BST is one hour ahead of GMT (UTC+1). If you fail to account for that, your time zone conversion will be one hour off.

Advertising [...] Advertising  

## How UTC Is Measured

Given that so much depends on UTC, it’s no surprise that significant effort goes into ensuring its precision.

Two components are used to keep it ticking at exactly the right pace:

   International Atomic Time (TAI): A time scale that combines the output of some 450 highly precise atomic clocks worldwide.  
   Universal Time (UT1): Also known as astronomical time or solar time, it refers to the Earth’s rotation. It is used to compare the pace provided by TAI with the actual length of a day on Earth.  

To reconcile the ultra-precise speed of atomic clocks with the fluctuations of Earth’s rotation, a leap second is added to or removed from UTC when the difference between the two components is predicted to reach 0.9 seconds within 12 months.
